listening.title: Part 2 · A walking tour of the old harbour
listening.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
script: Welcome, everyone, to this afternoon's walking tour of the old harbour. My name's Owen, and I've been a guide here for about eight years. Before we start, a few practical points. The tour lasts roughly ninety minutes, and we'll finish at the lighthouse rather than back here, so do keep that in mind if you've parked your car nearby.

Now, a little history. The harbour was built in the eighteen-forties, mainly to export grain. People often assume it was built for fishing, but in fact the fishing fleet only became important about fifty years later, when the railway arrived and fresh fish could be sent to the cities overnight.

Our first stop will be the Custom House. Today it's a small museum, and entry is free, although they do ask visitors for a donation. Inside, the most popular item is not the old ship models, as you might expect, but a set of letters written by a harbour master's daughter, describing a great storm in eighteen ninety-four.

After that we'll walk along the north pier. Please stay on the inner side of the path, because the outer edge can be slippery, even in dry weather. Halfway along, you'll see a row of small cottages. These were originally built for the families of lifeboat crews, so they could reach the boat quickly when the alarm sounded.

Finally, a word about the lighthouse. It's still in use, but it has been fully automatic since nineteen eighty-two, so no one lives there any more. On the first Sunday of each month the tower is open to the public, which sadly isn't today, but we'll have a good view from the outside. Right, if there are no questions, let's set off.

reading.title: The Return of the Urban Beekeeper
paragraphs: A. Twenty years ago, keeping bees in the middle of a city would have seemed an eccentric hobby. Today, hives can be found on the roofs of hotels, office blocks and even railway stations in London, Paris, New York and Dublin. Supporters describe urban beekeeping as a simple way for city dwellers to reconnect with nature, and many companies now advertise their rooftop hives as proof of their commitment to the environment.

B. Part of the appeal lies in the surprising quality of city honey. Because gardens, parks and streets contain a wide mixture of plants, from lime trees to window boxes, urban bees often produce honey with a more varied flavour than bees kept beside a single crop in the countryside. In some cities, honey from rooftop hives sells at premium prices, and local beekeeping associations report long waiting lists for their beginners' courses.

C. However, the rapid growth of urban hives has started to worry some ecologists. Honeybees are only one of many bee species, and in most countries the majority of bee species are wild, living alone or in small colonies. Several studies have suggested that when honeybee hives become very dense, they may compete with these wild bees for the same flowers. Researchers in one European capital found that areas with the highest number of hives tended to have fewer wild bees, although they stressed that this pattern did not on its own prove that the honeybees were the cause.

D. Disease is a second concern. Honeybees can carry viruses and parasites, and a large number of colonies in a small area may make it easier for these to spread. Experienced beekeepers argue that well-managed hives pose little risk, but they admit that some newcomers do not inspect their colonies often enough to notice problems early.

E. For this reason, a number of conservation groups now encourage a different approach. Instead of adding more hives, they suggest that people who want to help pollinators should plant flowers that bloom at different times of the year, leave small areas of grass uncut, and avoid using chemical sprays. These measures benefit honeybees too, but they are particularly valuable for wild species, which often depend on specific plants and cannot travel far to find food.

F. None of this means that urban beekeeping should stop. Many experts believe it has real educational value, especially when schools are involved, because it helps children understand where food comes from. The challenge, they say, is to make sure that the number of hives in any one area matches the amount of food available. As one researcher put it, a city full of beehives but short of flowers is not a sign of a healthy environment.

We'll meet at nine o'clock in the car park beside the old coastguard station. Please don't go to the main beach entrance, because the café there is being rebuilt and the area is closed. Gloves and bags will be provided, but we ask everyone to bring their own drinking water, as we're trying to avoid plastic bottles altogether.

After the clean-up, at around one o'clock, there'll be free soup for all volunteers at the sailing club. And finally, if you can't come on the day but still want to help, you can make a donation on our website, which helps us pay for the skips that take the rubbish away.

reading.title: Why We Sleep on Our Memories
paragraphs: A. For most of history, sleep was regarded as a period of rest in which the brain simply switched off. Over the past few decades, however, researchers have shown that the sleeping brain is remarkably active, and that one of its most important jobs may be to strengthen and organise the memories formed during the day.

B. A typical night's sleep is made up of several cycles, each lasting roughly ninety minutes. Within each cycle the brain passes through lighter stages, a stage of deep or 'slow-wave' sleep, and a stage known as rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, during which most vivid dreaming takes place. Deep sleep tends to dominate the early part of the night, while REM periods become longer towards the morning.

C. Experiments suggest that these stages may support different kinds of memory. In a common type of study, volunteers learn a list of word pairs in the evening and are tested the next morning. Those who sleep normally usually remember more than those who are kept awake, and the improvement appears to be linked particularly to the amount of deep sleep they get. Skills such as playing a musical sequence also improve overnight, sometimes without any further practice at all.

D. One explanation is that during deep sleep the brain 'replays' patterns of activity recorded while we were awake. Studies in rats, in which electrodes measured the activity of individual brain cells, found that the same patterns seen as the animals explored a maze reappeared during later sleep, but at a much faster speed. Many scientists believe this replay helps transfer information from short-term storage to more permanent networks.

E. Sleep may also help us forget. The brain cannot keep every detail of every day, and some researchers argue that sleep allows unimportant connections between brain cells to weaken, making room for new learning. This idea remains debated, but it could explain why people who are short of sleep often find it hard to take in new information.

F. These findings have practical consequences. Students who stay up all night before an exam may be damaging the very memories they are trying to protect. Short daytime naps have also been shown to improve learning in some studies, although naps that are too long can leave people feeling groggy. As one sleep scientist puts it, sleep is not the opposite of studying; it is part of it.

script: Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about the changes at the Central Library. As many of you know, the building reopened last month after a two-year renovation, and I'd like to explain some of the new services.

First, opening hours. We now stay open until eight o'clock on weekdays, which is two hours later than before. On Sundays, however, we're still closed, as staff numbers don't yet allow us to open seven days a week.

The biggest change is on the top floor, where we've created what we call the Maker Space. It has 3D printers, sewing machines and a small recording studio. Members can use the equipment for free, but you need to complete a short safety session first, which runs every Wednesday afternoon.

Many of you have asked about the children's section. It has moved from the basement to the ground floor, next to the café, so it's much easier to reach with a buggy. Story time for under-fives is now on Friday mornings instead of Mondays.

We've also changed the way fines work. From this month there are no fines for late books at all. Instead, if a book is more than four weeks late, you simply can't borrow anything else until it's returned. We found that fines were stopping some families from using the library.

Finally, a reminder that you can now renew books and book study rooms through our new app, rather than by phone. If you need help setting it up, our staff at the information desk will be happy to show you.

reading.title: Salt: The Mineral That Shaped History
paragraphs: A. Today salt is so cheap and easy to find that it is hard to imagine it was once one of the most valuable goods in the world. Yet for thousands of years, before refrigeration, salt was essential for preserving meat and fish through the winter, and the ability to produce or control it brought great wealth and power.

B. Early societies obtained salt in several ways. People living near the sea let seawater evaporate in shallow pools, a method still used in parts of France and Portugal today. Inland, salt was either cut from underground deposits or produced by boiling water from salty springs. Each method required considerable labour or fuel, which helps to explain why salt was traded over such long distances.

C. The importance of salt is reflected in language. A popular story claims that Roman soldiers were paid in salt and that this is the origin of the word 'salary'. Historians point out that there is little direct evidence for this, but the Latin word for salary is certainly related to the word for salt, perhaps because it referred to money given to buy it.

D. Because people could not live without salt, governments found it an ideal thing to tax. In France, a hated salt tax known as the gabelle was charged for centuries, and the amount people paid differed greatly from one region to another. The resulting resentment is often listed among the many causes of the French Revolution, after which the tax was abolished, although it was later brought back.

E. Perhaps the best-known protest against a salt tax took place in India in 1930. British law gave the colonial government control over salt production, and Mahatma Gandhi chose this law as the focus of a campaign of non-violent resistance. Together with his followers, he walked for more than three weeks to the coast at Dandi, where he picked up a handful of natural salt in a symbolic act of defiance. The march attracted attention around the world.

F. The arrival of modern refrigeration and industrial mining in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries finally made salt cheap. Today the largest share of salt produced worldwide is not eaten at all; it is used by the chemical industry and to keep roads free of ice in winter. Doctors, meanwhile, warn that many people now eat too much of it, a problem that earlier generations could hardly have imagined.

script: Hello and welcome to the visitor centre at Glenmore National Park. I'm Sinéad, one of the rangers, and I'd like to give you some information before you set off.

The park covers around sixteen thousand hectares, and most of it is mountain and bog. The visitor centre itself was opened in two thousand and ten, but the park is much older: it was created in the nineteen eighties to protect the red deer, which had almost disappeared from the area.

There are three marked walking trails. The blue trail is the shortest and is suitable for wheelchairs and buggies. The red trail goes up to the waterfall and takes about two hours. The black trail climbs to the top of the mountain, and we only recommend it for experienced walkers with proper boots.
Please remember that dogs are allowed in the park, but they must be kept on a lead at all times, because the deer are giving birth at this time of year.

The café here in the visitor centre serves hot food until four o'clock. After that, only drinks and snacks are available. If you're planning a picnic, please take all your rubbish home with you, because there are no bins on the trails.

Finally, the weather here can change very quickly. If you're doing the red or black trail, please tell a member of staff before you leave, and check the board at the entrance, which shows today's weather warnings.

reading.title: How Habits Are Made
paragraphs: A. Much of what we do each day is not the result of careful decisions but of habit. Researchers who asked volunteers to record their actions every hour found that a large share of daily behaviour, from the route people took to work to the snacks they ate, was performed in the same place and in the same way almost every day.

B. Psychologists often describe a habit as a loop with three parts. First comes a cue, such as a time of day, a place or a feeling. This triggers a routine, the behaviour itself, which is followed by some kind of reward. Over time, the brain begins to link the cue directly with the reward, so that the routine starts almost automatically, with very little conscious thought.

C. A popular belief holds that it takes twenty-one days to form a new habit. However, this figure appears to come from a 1960s book by a surgeon describing how patients adjusted to changes in their appearance, not from a study of habits. When researchers in London followed people trying to adopt simple new behaviours, such as drinking a glass of water after breakfast, they found that the time needed varied enormously, from a few weeks to many months, with an average of around two months.

D. The same study offered some comfort to anyone who has broken a good intention. Missing a single day did not seem to harm the process in the long run. What mattered more was repeating the behaviour in a consistent setting, so that the cue became strongly connected to the action.

E. This helps to explain why changes in environment can be so powerful. People who move house or start a new job often find it easier to drop old habits, because the familiar cues have disappeared. Some experts recommend taking advantage of such moments to introduce healthier routines.

F. Breaking a bad habit, on the other hand, is usually harder than starting a good one. Rather than relying on willpower alone, many psychologists suggest changing the cue or making the unwanted behaviour less convenient. Keeping sweets out of sight, for example, may work better than simply promising not to eat them.

listening.title: Part 2 · The new city bike scheme
listening.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
script: Good evening. I'm here from the city council to explain how our new bike-sharing scheme will work when it launches in March.

To begin with, there will be forty stations across the city centre, with around five hundred bikes in total. About a third of the bikes will be electric, which should help people who live on the hills to the north of the river.

To use a bike, you'll need to download the app and register a bank card. An annual subscription costs thirty euros, and that gives you the first thirty minutes of every journey free. Longer trips cost fifty cent for each extra half hour.
We know that safety is a concern. Every bike has lights that switch on automatically, and helmets are not provided, so we strongly encourage users to bring their own.

One question we're often asked is what happens if a station is full when you arrive. In that case, the app will show you the nearest station with free spaces and give you fifteen extra minutes at no cost to get there.
Finally, during the first month, students will be able to use the scheme for free. After that they'll pay half the normal price for a subscription.

reading.title: The Long Journey of Coffee
paragraphs: A. Coffee is now one of the most widely traded farm products in the world, yet its early history is surprisingly uncertain. The coffee plant is native to the forests of Ethiopia, and a well-known legend tells of a goat herder who noticed that his animals became unusually lively after eating its red berries. Historians treat this story with caution, since it was first written down many centuries after the events it describes.

B. What is clearer is that by the fifteenth century coffee was being drunk in Yemen, on the other side of the Red Sea. There, members of religious communities used it to help them stay awake during night-time prayers. From Yemen, the drink spread to Mecca, Cairo and later Istanbul, where public coffee houses became popular meeting places.

C. These coffee houses were not always welcome. Because people gathered in them to talk, play games and discuss the news, rulers sometimes suspected them of encouraging political criticism. On several occasions authorities tried to close them, but such bans rarely lasted long.

D. Coffee reached Europe in the seventeenth century, largely through trade with the Ottoman Empire. Coffee houses soon opened in Venice, London and Paris. In London they became known as places where merchants met to do business, and some well-known institutions, including an early insurance market, are said to have grown out of conversations in coffee houses.

E. For a long time, almost all the world's coffee came from Yemen, which tried to prevent fertile seeds from leaving the country. Eventually, however, plants were taken to colonies in Asia and later to the Caribbean and South America. Today Brazil is by far the largest producer, followed by Vietnam.

F. Coffee's success has brought problems as well as pleasure. Many of the farmers who grow it earn very little, and prices can rise or fall sharply from one year to the next. Scientists also warn that rising temperatures could reduce the land suitable for growing coffee in the coming decades, which has led researchers to search for wild varieties that can survive in hotter conditions.

listening.title: Part 2 · The Saturday farmers' market
listening.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
script: Hi everyone, and welcome to this short talk about our town's farmers' market, which celebrates its tenth birthday this year.

The market started with just six stalls in the church car park. It soon became too big for that space, and since two thousand and nineteen it has been held in the old fish market building by the river, which gives us shelter when it rains.

We now have around forty stalls. To keep a place, every trader must sell food they have grown, raised or made themselves, and they must be based within fifty kilometres of the town. This rule is checked by visits to the farms.

The market is open every Saturday from nine until two. Many people think the best time to come is early, but actually some of our traders reduce their prices in the last half hour, so if you're looking for a bargain, come just before closing.

This year we've introduced two new things. First, there's a cookery demonstration at eleven o'clock each week, using ingredients from the stalls. Second, we now have a scheme where you can bring back your glass jars, which are cleaned and reused by the honey and jam makers.
And one last request: please don't bring dogs inside the building. There's a covered area outside where you can leave them safely while you shop.

reading.title: Why Cities Are Planting Trees
paragraphs: A. On a hot summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This effect, known as the urban heat island, occurs because roads, roofs and walls absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, while there are fewer plants to provide shade and cooling.

B. Trees help to reduce this heat in two main ways. Their leaves block sunlight before it reaches the ground, and they release water vapour through tiny openings in their leaves, a process that cools the surrounding air. Measurements in many cities have shown that streets lined with mature trees can be noticeably cooler than similar streets without them.

C. The benefits go beyond temperature. Trees catch some rainwater on their leaves and help the soil absorb more of it, which can reduce flooding during heavy storms. They also provide homes for birds and insects, and several studies have linked access to green spaces with lower levels of stress among city residents.

D. As a result, many cities have announced ambitious planting targets. Some aim to cover a certain percentage of their area with tree canopy, the layer formed by the leaves and branches when seen from above, by a fixed date. Others focus on neighbourhoods that have the fewest trees, which are often poorer areas.

E. However, planting a tree is only the beginning. Young trees need regular watering for their first few years, and a significant number die before they become established, especially when they are planted in small pits surrounded by concrete. Experts therefore argue that cities should measure success not by the number of trees planted, but by the number that survive and grow.

F. Choosing the right species also matters. A tree that grows well today may struggle as summers become hotter and drier, so planners are increasingly selecting a wider variety of species. Mixing species also reduces the risk that a single disease could destroy a large share of a city's trees at once, as happened in many places when elm trees were lost to disease in the twentieth century.
